source_text: Sed enim vera et tota et pura virginitas nihil magis timet quam semetipsam. Etiam feminarum oculos pati non vult. Alios ipsa oculos habet. Confugit ad velamen capitis quasi ad galeam, quasi ad clypeum, qui bonum suum protegat adversus ictus temptationum, adversus iacula scandalorum, adversus suspiciones et susurros et aemulationem, ipsum quoque livorem. Nam est aliquid etiam apud ethnicos metuendum, quod fascinum vocant, infeliciorem laudis et gloriae enormioris eventum. Hoc nos interdum diabolo interpretamur, ipsius est enim boni odium; interdum deo deputamus, illius est enim superbiae iudicium, extollentis humiles et deprimentis elatos. Timebit itaque virgo sanctior, vel in nomine fascini, hinc adversarium, inde deum, illius lividum ingenium, huius censorium lumen, et gaudebit sibi soli et deo nota. Sed et si cui innotuerit, sapit si temptationibus gradum obstruxerit. Quis enim audebit oculis suis premere faciem clausam, faciem non sentientem, faciem, ut dixerim, tristem? Quicunque malus cogitatus ipsa severitate frangetur. Iam se etiam mulierem negat quae virginem celat.
thought_title: True virginity fears itself and hides
orientation: Tertullian is describing how a true virgin protects her modesty by veiling, after arguing that unveiled virgins are endangered by public attention.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed true and whole and pure virginity fears nothing more than itself. Even the eyes of women it is not willing to endure. Other eyes it itself has. It flees to the veil of the head as to a helmet, as to a shield, which may protect its good against the blows of temptations, against the darts of scandals, against suspicions and whispers and rivalry, also envy itself. For there is something also among the heathens to be feared, which they call the evil eye, an event more unhappy of praise and of glory more excessive. This we sometimes interpret to the devil, for his is the hatred of good; sometimes we assign to God, for his is the judgment of pride, who exalts the humble and casts down the proud. Therefore the holier virgin will fear, even in the name of the evil eye, on this side the adversary, on that side God, the envious disposition of the one, the censoring light of the other, and she will rejoice to be known to herself alone and to God. But even if she becomes known to anyone, she is wise if she blocks the way to temptations. For who will dare with his eyes to press a closed face, a face not feeling, a face, as I might say, sad? Whatever evil thought will be broken by that very severity. Now she denies that she is even a woman who conceals a virgin.

choices.why: The term refers to the pagan belief in harm caused by envious or excessive praise; 'evil eye' captures the superstition Tertullian names.
Keeps the literal phrase 'of the head' to match the source and the glossary term 'veil'.
Literal rendering of the participle; the face is presented as unresponsive to gazes.
rejected: a face that does not feel

choices.english: she is wise if she blocks the way to temptations
choices.why: Keeps the conditional force and the metaphor of blocking a step or path.
rejected: she acts wisely by blocking temptations
she is sensible to block the approach of temptations

choices.english: she denies that she is even a woman who conceals a virgin
choices.why: Preserves the paradox: by hiding her virginity, she refuses the public status of 'woman'.
rejected: she who hides a virgin denies being a woman

pass_b_english: But true, complete, and pure virginity fears nothing more than itself. It refuses to endure even the eyes of women; it has eyes of its own. It flees for refuge to the veil of the head as to a helmet, as to a shield, to protect its good against the blows of temptations, against the darts of scandals, against suspicions and whispers and rivalry, and against envy itself. For there is something to be feared even among the pagans which they call the evil eye, a most unhappy outcome of excessive praise and glory. We sometimes interpret this as the devil, since hatred of good belongs to him; sometimes we attribute it to God, since judgment of pride belongs to Him, who exalts the humble and casts down the proud. Therefore the holier virgin will fear, even in the name of the evil eye, the adversary on one side and God on the other—the one's spiteful nature, the other's censoring light—and she will rejoice to be known to herself alone and to God. But even if she becomes known to someone, she is wise if she bars the way against temptations. For who will dare to press with his eyes upon a closed face, a face not feeling, a face, so to speak, sad? Every evil thought will be broken by that very severity. Now she who conceals a virgin denies that she is even a woman.

problems.quote: she is wise if she blocks the way to temptations
problems.why: The dative means she bars temptations' approach to her, not her path toward temptations.
problems.fix: she is wise if she bars the way against temptations
problems.ruling: Dative 'temptationibus' with 'gradum obstruxerit' means she bars temptations' advance. 'Blocks the way to temptations' reverses the direction and the agency.

edits.old: she is wise if she blocks the way to temptations
edits.new: she is wise if she bars the way against temptations

fixed: agency: fixed — 'temptationibus gradum obstruxerit' has temptationibus as dative blocking their approach, so 'bars the way against temptations'.
